newsitem.title: UK: European car sales to stall in 97, price war seen.
newsitem.headline: European car sales to stall in 97, price war seen.

text.p: European car sales are set to stall in 1997 as the French and Italian markets stay locked in recession, leading to the outbreak of a new price war due to excess capacity in a dead market, said a survey on Monday.

The gloomy findings were reported in a survey of the car industry from J D Power-LMC, part of an international Oxford-based consultancy. It said consumer demand would suffer next year as European governments seek to raise taxes to try to meet budgetary requirements to qualify for monetary union in 1999.

"European car demand will stall in 1997 with France and Italy both in recession," said Arthur Maher, head of European forecasting. "European car production will remain flat with excess capacity threatening a new price war," added research director Charles Young.
The growth areas cited are Asia, South America and Eastern Europe which are expected to expand by 25 percent or more.

But Europe looks bleak. Growth this year of 6.8 percent has been attributed to government incentives including the French moves to encourage scrapping old fuel-guzzling cars in favour of new models. This factor has artificially boosted sales growth by one third, said the survey.
Next year European growth will be two percent. In a market breakdown, the report said French car makers like PSA and Renault would suffer a 10 percent crash in domestic sales.
Sales would also suffer in Italy, hampering car maker Fiat, and German growth would slow, said the report, hit by rising unemployment and a weak German economy.
The UK market remained healthier, but there was concern that the market might peak as economic measures were tightened after the general election due by May 1997.

New medium term threats to European car makers included competitive challenges from Korea, removal of remaining constraints on Japanese vehicle exports to Europe from 2000 and an expected European cyclical downturn in 2000.
